governor-wall.name: Governor’s Residence Wall
governor-wall.lead: A trace on the wall that tells the town's story

then.headline: The governor's camp wall in a tin-mining town by the sea route
then.body:
The Takua Pa governor's residence wall is suggested, not settled, to have been built during the time of Phraya Senanuchit (Nuch Na Nakhon), the governor of Takua Pa, between 1840 and 1881 (2383-2424 BE). However, academic sources have not yet specified the exact starting year of construction. The wall enclosed the residence and official areas, functioning like a fortified camp to protect against enemies and serve as a shelter for the townspeople.

This was the period when Takua Pa grew from the tin mining economy and coastal trade. The old town was located along the Takua Pa River, connecting to the Andaman Sea and multinational trade networks. The Chinese community who came to mine and trade played an important role, but conflicts over tin mining interests meant that a secure stronghold was necessary. The wall was therefore both the ruler's home and a tool for maintaining peace in the town.

The interior layout is divided into three parts: the front palace, the hall, and the rear palace, with connecting doors. It was built with lime mixed with gravel and sand laid in layers, with a base wider than the wall itself. The intact parts are about 5 meters high. Evidence from later excavations revealed Qing Dynasty Chinese ceramics, European ceramics, and contemporary materials, reflecting the town's trade contacts in that era.

before.headline: From a lived-in residence to a historical site protected by the old town
before.body:
After Phraya Senanuchit (Nuch) left office, the wall and residence continued to be used during the time of Phraya Senanuchit (Iam Na Nakhon) between 1881 and 1892. King Chulalongkorn visited Takua Pa and viewed this residence on May 28, 1890.

Later, when the town center was relocated to Ko Kho Khao and Ban Yan Yao during the time of Phra Narathep Phakdi (Sit Na Nakhon), the former residence lost its official role and was likely abandoned from then on. Verified sources did not find evidence confirming that the wall was used for other businesses or was directly damaged by the 2004 tsunami.

The Fine Arts Department registered it as a historical site and defined the land boundaries in the Royal Gazette on December 18, 1996. It was later excavated and restored in 1999, prior to recent landscape improvements. Current sources indicate that the wall is more stable, but still has weeds and roots in some spots that require care.

now.headline: A living historical site: the old wall becomes Takua Pa's stage
now.body:
Today, the Takua Pa governor's residence wall is a historical site that is open to the public every day with no admission fee. The archaeological database lists joint caretakers including the Fine Arts Department, Takua Pa Town Municipality, and the Na Nakhon family. Inside, there is a lawn and some walkways, along with information boards from the Fine Arts Department and the Tourism Authority of Thailand.

The area no longer functions as the governor's residence, but it continues to act as a landmark for the old town and a space for community ceremonies and activities. During 2026, Phang Nga Province and Takua Pa Town Municipality organized the 12th "From Takola to Takua Pa" event at the residence from February 28 to March 3. The event featured Khon, Nora, shadow puppetry, worship ceremonies, Buddhist chanting, as well as the sale of local food and OTOP products.

Its contemporary use is therefore for heritage tourism and learning about the Takua Pa way of life. At the same time, some parts of the wall remain damaged with clinging plants. Verified official sources have not announced a new restoration project or specific budget details for 2026.

khun-in.name: Khun In House
khun-in.lead: Windows and balconies serve as an entryway to the house's history

then.headline: The district chief's house in a tin port town
then.body:
Local evidence indicates that Khun In House was built around 1917 (2460 BE) by Chinese craftsmen. It served as the residence of Lieutenant Khun Intharakhiri (Choi Na Nakhon), a descendant of the governor's family who later became the Takua Pa district chief between 1921 and 1926. It is therefore not just a beautiful building, but the home of an individual who played a role in the town's administrative structure during the transition from the governor system to the district system.

This house was established in Takua Pa, a town that grew from trade and tin mining. The town relied on rivers and canals as transportation routes, with trade ships from China and Myanmar coming in to exchange goods, and many Thai-Chinese and Hokkien Chinese settling down. The two-story brick and mortar applied Sino-Portuguese architecture thus reflects both the homeowner's status and the Andaman trade world that connected Takua Pa with people of many cultures.

In the town at that time, the house functioned as the residence of a senior official and was part of the old town landscape that included wealthy merchants' houses, shops, and religious sites. However, primary documents detailing the exact starting date of construction, names of the craftsmen, or other direct public functions of the house have not yet been found.

before.headline: From a family home to an old town heritage
before.body:
After decades of use, the building deteriorated before the Na Nakhon family repaired it around 1981, adhering primarily to the original design and replacing the tortoise-shell-like roof tiles with corrugated tiles. This is the conservation event with the clearest specified year for Khun In House from accessible sources.

Meanwhile, Takua Pa transformed from a tin mining and water trade center into a quieter town as the old economy declined. Rivers and canals became shallow from mining activities, and the old community gradually shifted its role toward a cultural and tourist district. Khun In House was thus remembered alongside the cultural street, Chinese-European buildings, and evidence of the old mining town.

The official database of ONEP classifies Khun In House as an architectural art site, and the SAC community database lists it among the historical sites of Takua Pa. However, a review of accessible sources did not find the year it was registered as a historical site by the Fine Arts Department, its use for other businesses, or evidence that the house was damaged by the 2004 tsunami.

now.headline: A heritage building still under family care
now.body:
The verified status in 2026 is that Khun In House is still mentioned as a historical building in the Takua Pa old town, and local sources indicate that it remains under the care of the Na Nakhon family. The building holds value for its applied Sino-Portuguese style and its historical connection with Khun Intharakhiri.

The house does not have public information confirming opening hours, admission fees, on-site caretakers, or the official opening of the interior spaces. It should therefore be considered a building to be appreciated from the outside, as the status of interior visits remains unknown. It should not be concluded that it is a museum or a regular event venue.

Today, the house serves a symbolic role in the old town landscape, coexisting with the cultural street and other historical buildings in the community. Unlike projects with clear announcements, no news or announcements from 2022 to 2026 have been found specifying restorations or activities exclusively for Khun In House.

tao-ming.name: Tao Ming School
tao-ming.lead: A school building that tells a story of cultural transmission

then.headline: From mining town donations to Takua Pa's first Chinese school
then.body:
Before having a permanent building, Tao Ming School unofficially taught Chinese as a private entity. When the Private Schools Act of 1918 (2461 BE) took effect, the school officially requested establishment in 1920 under the name "Toh Beng" in the Hokkien dialect, before changing to "Tao Ming" in Mandarin. The word carries the conceptual meaning of guiding towards knowledge.

The building that can still be seen was constructed in 1922 with donations from tin mining millionaires and Chinese merchants in the old market, the Yan Yao area, and merchant networks from Ranong and Phuket. Another official source explains that it was the work of the Chinese Merchants Association who came to mine tin, providing a place for Chinese descendants to learn the Chinese language. The applied Sino-Portuguese building with a zinc roof was therefore not just a school, but evidence that the wealth from mining, trade, and Chinese networks was transforming into a community institution.

At that time, Takua Pa was a trade and transportation hub tied to the river and the sea. The town grew from tin ore, with Chinese from Fujian, Guangdong, and Hainan arriving as laborers, merchants, and entrepreneurs. The school functioned to instil linguistic and cultural roots for the Chinese community in the thriving mining town.

before.headline: When the mining town quieted down, the school paused, but the building still speaks
before.body:
Local sources indicate that the Takua Pa tin mines gradually shut down from the 1970s, reducing the town's liveliness, while Tao Ming School subsequently ceased operations. Verified official sources only confirm that "the school has been discontinued" and the building is under the care of the Tao Ming School Foundation, Takua Pa, but do not specify the year of closure or details of the handover.

No accessible evidence has been found to confirm that the building was directly affected by the 2004 tsunami, or if any restoration occurred in a specific year. Therefore, it should not be concluded that it was damaged or repaired due to that event, even though the Takua Pa area had locations involved in managing tsunami victims and the old town revived its role in cultural tourism.

The old town boundary document from ONEP shows the boundary passing through Tao Ming School, and the SAC community database lists the building as a key evidence of the old town. However, this search has not yet found a Fine Arts Department announcement specifically registering the "Tao Ming School Building," thus separating the conservation status of the district from the registration status of the building itself.

now.headline: The original building remains in the old town, but it is no longer an active school
now.body:
The verified status today is that the school has closed, leaving a historic building under the care of the Tao Ming School Foundation, Takua Pa. It is important to understand that "visiting the building" does not equate to "visiting an active school."

The building is located on Si Takua Pa Road in the old town and is still used as a destination in tourism media by the municipality, the Tourism Authority of Thailand, and old town activities, such as the Cultural Street held on Si Takua Pa Road. The found information confirms the context of activities in the area, but it is not verified if events are regularly held inside the building.

The condition confirmed by official sources is that the building remains and holds architectural value in the applied Sino-Portuguese style. However, opening hours, admission fees, regular caretakers, interior access, wheelchair accessibility, and any restoration projects for 2026 lack verifiable public data. Therefore, one should contact the caretaker or municipality before traveling.

new-year-alms.name: New Year's Dawn Almsgiving
new-year-alms.lead: A merit-making activity to welcome the new year

then.headline: The starting point cannot yet be determined from the found evidence
then.body:
For the event named 'New Year's Dawn Almsgiving', no documents have been found that directly state the starting year, the initiator, or the initial ceremony. Therefore, it cannot be responsibly narrated whether the event originated during the governor's era, the tin mining era, or from any specific community group.

The found evidence only confirms that in the Takua Pa Town Municipality's development plan tracking documents, there is a project to organize New Year's Day events and dried food almsgiving activities at the waterfront. However, the document does not specify the founding year, the name of the pier, or the founder.

The Takua Pa context in academic works is described as once prosperous from tin mining, and the old town features shophouses that reflect past trade. However, there is no evidence directly connecting this almsgiving activity to the tin mines, maritime trade, the Hokkien Chinese, or the governors. Therefore, its origin period is considered unverified.

before.headline: From a canceled New Year's event during COVID to the return of merit-making ceremonies in the old town
before.body:
In late 2020, local government organizations in Takua Pa District discussed 'canceling New Year's Day activities' that included almsgiving due to the COVID-19 situation. This evidence indicates that the event did not proceed consistently every year and the schedule depends on the situation and local decisions.

After that period, news evidence became clearer regarding almsgiving activities during the Songkran/Thai New Year festival in the Takua Pa old town, held on the Cultural Street and attended by the municipality, district officials, monks, locals, and tourists. This is evidence that the old town area still uses merit-making ceremonies as a community and cultural tourism activity, but it should not be conflated with the exact target event name.

There is no evidence that this activity was abandoned, restored, granted historical site status, or directly affected by the 2004 tsunami, because what was found is an 'activity', not a permanent building or location.

now.headline: Almsgiving ceremonies are still held in the area, but the location and schedule for this event name remain unfixed
now.body:
As of 2026, almsgiving ceremonies are still found in Takua Pa District. News from April 13, 2026, reported an almsgiving of rice and dried food at the Takua Pa old town Songkran event, attended by monks, government agencies, citizens, and tourists. This activity reflects the actual use of the old town area as a cultural stage, but it was for the Thai New Year during Songkran, not direct evidence of a January 1st event.

Regarding the name 'New Year's Dawn Almsgiving', there is still no verified information that it is organized in 2026, at which location, at what time, or who specifically oversees the event. Therefore, it cannot be concluded if it is regularly open for participation or has a permanent location. Those interested in participating should check the announcements from Takua Pa Town Municipality and Takua Pa District before traveling.

No evidence was found in this research round regarding restoration projects, visitor service points, admission fees, building conditions, or facilities, because the target is a traditional event, not a building.
